seo.title: uv Python Tutorial #4 — One File, No Setup: PEP 723 Scripts (2026)
altTitles: Self-contained Python scripts with uv and inline metadata
seo.description: Chapter four of the uv course. uv run --with, PEP 723 inline metadata, uv init --script and uv add --script, the uv run shebang, locking a script, and why the surrounding project is ignored.
seo.breakdown: PEP 723 inline metadata — four comment lines that let one Python file carry its own environment and run anywhere.

scenes.narration: One Python file. No project, no setup, no install step. It just runs.

Watch the clock on this one. A single file sits on this machine, and rich is installed absolutely nowhere. I run the file, uv reads the file, uv builds whatever the file asks for, and the output appears on screen. One point eight seconds, from nothing at all. So where did rich come from?

uvStage.headline: Nothing to [output], in 1.8s
uvStage.premise: One file. rich installed in no environment anywhere on this machine.

steps.label: ls
steps.detail: one file. nothing else in the folder.

steps.label: time uv run demo.py
out: Reading inline script metadata from: demo.py
steps.detail: no project. no venv. no install step.

steps.label: uv pip list
steps.detail: and rich is still installed nowhere

scenes.narration: Welcome back. This chapter is about the smallest useful thing in the whole of uv: a single file that carries its own dependencies and needs nothing else on the machine to work.

data.title: A script that fixes itself
data.subtitle: uv, chapter four · one file, no setup

scenes.narration: Start at the simplest possible version, then work up to that demo.

Typing uv run and a filename runs that file. Where a project already has an environment, uv'll reach for that one. Where a package is missing, you can lend the script one for a single run with dash dash with — exactly the way you lent a tool a plugin two chapters back.

uvStage.headline: Lend it a package, [once]
uvStage.premise: --with adds a package for this one run and changes nothing on disk.

steps.label: uv run demo.py
steps.detail: rich is not on any shelf here

steps.label: uv run --with rich demo.py
steps.detail: borrowed for exactly one run

steps.label: uv pip show rich
out: warning: Package(s) not found for: rich
steps.detail: and gone again immediately afterwards

scenes.narration: Lending works, but lending is fragile, because the knowledge of what the script needs lives in your head and in your shell history. Send the file to a colleague and your colleague gets the same module error you got. The fix, then, has to put that knowledge inside the file itself.

uvStage.headline: The knowledge is in [your head]
uvStage.premise: The file says nothing about what it needs, so the file cannot travel alone.

steps.label: scp demo.py them@laptop:~/
steps.detail: the file goes. the flag does not.

stage.label: them
stage.sub: they get the module error you got

scenes.narration: So: how do you write requirements inside a Python file that Python itself will ignore?

There's a real Python standard for exactly this, and it's beautifully simple. Put a block of comments at the very top of the file, opened by slash slash slash script and closed by slash slash slash. Python skips the entire block, because comments are comments and the interpreter doesn't care what's inside them. uv reads the very same block and builds an environment out of the contents.

uvStage.headline: A comment Python [ignores]
uvStage.premise: Comments to Python. Instructions to uv. The same four lines do both jobs.

steps.label: head -5 demo.py
steps.detail: four comment lines, and a whole environment

stage.label: # dependencies = ["rich"]
stage.sub: and what goes on its shelf

scenes.narration: You never have to type that block by hand. Running uv init dash dash script writes the block for you, and uv add dash dash script edits the block in place afterwards. Which means adding a dependency to a lone file is the same gesture as adding one to a whole project.

uvStage.headline: uv writes the [header] for you
uvStage.premise: Two commands create and edit the block, so nobody hand-edits comments.

steps.label: uv init --script demo.py --python 3.12
steps.detail: the block is written, dependencies empty

steps.label: uv add --script demo.py rich
steps.detail: and now the block names rich

steps.label: head -4 demo.py
steps.detail: uv edited the comments, in place

scenes.narration: Now here's the part that makes people sit up. My init command asked for Python three point twelve, and three point twelve was not on this machine anywhere. uv simply downloaded an entire Python — twenty-one megabytes of interpreter — and carried on without stopping to ask.

uvStage.headline: It fetched a whole [Python]
uvStage.premise: 3.12 was not on this machine, so uv fetched one rather than refusing.

steps.label: uv init --script demo.py --python 3.12
steps.detail: this is chapter one paying off

scenes.narration: And none of that would be possible without what chapter one explained. uv is a binary standing beside Python, which means uv can go and fetch a Python. A tool written in Python couldn't manage the same trick, because it'd need an interpreter before it could start looking for one.

uvStage.headline: This is [chapter one] paying off
uvStage.premise: A tool inside Python cannot fetch a Python. A binary beside it can.
uvStage.stageTitle: why uv can do this at all

steps.label: uv python install 3.12
steps.detail: a Rust binary fetching an interpreter

stage.label: pip
stage.sub: would need this first, to fetch this

scenes.narration: Two more things, and then the file becomes genuinely portable.

Put a shebang line at the very top and the file becomes runnable on its own. Mark the file executable, type dot slash demo dot py, and your operating system hands it straight to uv, which reads the header and does everything else. No python command typed anywhere.

uvStage.headline: Run it like [any] program
uvStage.premise: A shebang hands the file to uv, and uv reads the header before running it.

steps.label: chmod +x demo.py && ./demo.py
steps.detail: no python, no uv typed at all

scenes.narration: Now, the header names what the script needs, but not the exact versions, which means two people can still end up with slightly different parcels. Running uv lock dash dash script freezes those versions into a companion file beside the script, and from then on everybody who runs the file gets an identical set — the same guarantee a project lockfile gives you.

uvStage.headline: Freeze it with a [lockfile]
uvStage.premise: A companion file beside the script, holding the exact versions and hashes.

steps.label: uv lock --script demo.py
steps.detail: and a demo.py.lock appears beside it

stage.label: mdurl
stage.sub: and everyone gets these exact files

scenes.narration: One rule does catch people out, so it's worth saying plainly. When a file carries an inline header, the project around the file is ignored completely — the documentation says the project's dependencies will not be used. Which means a script sitting inside a project still gets a private shelf, built only from that script's own header.

uvStage.headline: The project is [ignored]
uvStage.premise: A header wins. The surrounding project contributes nothing to the script.

steps.label: uv add httpx
steps.detail: httpx is now a project dependency

steps.label: uv run demo.py
steps.detail: and the script still cannot see it

stage.label: wall
stage.sub: a header makes the script its own little world

scenes.narration: There's more that fits in the header than a package list. Requires-python sets the interpreter, exclude-newer freezes the whole resolution to a date, and a tool table can carry per-tool configuration. All of it still comments, and Python still ignores every line.

uvStage.headline: What else fits in the [block]
uvStage.premise: Still comments. Still ignored by Python. Considerably more useful than a list.

steps.label: uv run --exclude-newer 2026-01-01 demo.py
steps.detail: resolved as if today were January

stage.label: # exclude-newer
stage.sub: pretend nothing was published after a date

scenes.narration: And because everything lives inside the file, the second run's nearly free. uv keys that little environment on exactly what the header asked for, so as long as the header stays the same, the depot answers and nothing is fetched again.

uvStage.headline: The second run is [free] too
uvStage.premise: The environment is keyed on the header, so an unchanged header means no fetch.

steps.label: time uv run demo.py
steps.detail: first run: built from scratch

steps.label: time uv run demo.py
steps.detail: second run: the header had not changed

stage.label: second run
stage.sub: the same shelf was already standing

stage.label: change one line and it rebuilds

scenes.narration: Quick check. A script has an inline header naming rich, and it sits inside a project that depends on httpx. Can the script import httpx? Pause here and think it through before I answer. Ready? No — the header wins, and the project is ignored entirely.

quiz.question: Script has a header. Can it import the project’s packages?
quiz.why: Inline metadata makes the script its own world, project or no project.

scenes.narration: This is genuinely useful in real life. A one-file utility you can email to somebody. A build step in a repository that needs two libraries nobody wants in the main project. A snippet in a bug report that actually runs on the reader's machine. All of it from four comment lines.

uvStage.headline: Where this actually [pays off]
uvStage.premise: Three ordinary situations where a self-contained file beats a whole project.

steps.label: uv run https://example.com/tidy.py
steps.detail: uv will even run one straight off a URL

stage.label: email a utility
stage.sub: and it runs on their machine

stage.label: a repo build step
stage.sub: without adding to the main project

stage.label: a bug report
stage.sub: the reader can actually run your snippet

scenes.narration: So, to recap. To recap, then: a block of comments at the top of a file tells uv what the file needs, and Python ignores those comments completely. uv writes and edits that block for you. And if the Python you asked for is missing, uv fetches it rather than refusing.

points.text: Four comment lines carry the whole environment
uv writes and edits that block for you
Missing Python? uv fetches one and carries on.

scenes.narration: Next chapter we stop letting Python be something you install by hand, and let uv own every version on your machine instead.
